label: Job Loss
framing: Losing a job takes more than a paycheck. It can take the role you wore, the worth you measured by it, and the place you held in the world, and Scripture knows the difference between what you do and who you are.
cultural: Our culture asks a stranger what they do before it asks their name, and ties a person's dignity to their output and title. Scripture never makes that trade. It grounds your worth not in your productivity but in your bearing the image of God, a worth no layoff can issue or revoke, even as it honors real work as good and the loss of it as a real grief.
historical: Work has been disrupted in every age, by plague, by war, by the upheaval of the machines. The Reformers, Luther and Calvin among them in the sixteenth century, recovered the dignity of ordinary labor and called every honest calling a vocation, a place to serve God and neighbor. That conviction has sustained believers through every season when the work they loved was taken from them.
application: Grieve the loss honestly rather than rushing to look composed, for it is a real bereavement. Refuse the lie that your value walked out with your badge. Let the people who love you in, do the practical work of looking without letting it consume every hour, and keep a rhythm of rest and worship that reminds you who you are when no one is paying you to be it.

verses.text: About the eleventh hour he went out and found still others standing around. ‘Why have you been standing here all day long doing nothing?’ he asked. ‘Because no one has hired us,’ they answered. So he told them, ‘You also go into my vineyard.’
verses.where: At the eleventh hour the landowner finds men still standing in the marketplace, asks why, and they answer that no one has hired them. The site's note says he keeps going out and calls those no one else chose, and its teaching note says the story may touch people who know unemployment, or being the one no one picks. The note adds that the story does not blame them.

verses.text: The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.
verses.where: Joseph has helped Pharaoh's cupbearer, and the restored official forgets him; the next chapter opens two full years later. The site's note says Joseph had done everything right and was left in prison, his suffering extended by an ordinary human failing, and that the Bible does not pretend such delays do not hurt. The plain note asks whether someone forgot you when you needed them.

verses.text: Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s household.” And the second son he named Ephraim, saying, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
verses.where: Raised at last to serve Pharaoh, Joseph names his sons Manasseh, for God has made him forget his hardship, and Ephraim, for God has made him fruitful in the land of his affliction. The site's note says he credits God with healing the memory of his suffering, not erasing it. The plain note asks where God has made you fruitful in a place you never wanted to be.

verses.text: I saw something else under the sun: The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; neither is the bread to the wise, nor the wealth to the intelligent, nor the favor to the skillful. For time and chance happen to all.
verses.where: The Teacher observes that the race is not to the swift, nor the bread to the wise, nor the favor to the skillful, for time and chance happen to all. The site's note on the chapter names this observation and the story that follows, of a poor wise man who saved a city and was forgotten. A lost job is not always a verdict on the one who lost it.

verses.text: Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls, yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!
verses.where: At the end of his book Habakkuk imagines every crop and flock failing, the fields producing no food, and says he will still rejoice in the God of his salvation. The site's note on the chapter says that, trembling at what he has heard, he resolves to wait quietly and declares that even if every crop and flock fails he will rejoice in God. His joy is not in the harvest coming back but in God while it has not.

verses.text: And Ruth the Moabitess said to Naomi, “Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor.” “Go ahead, my daughter,” Naomi replied. So Ruth departed and went out into the field and gleaned after the harvesters. And she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech.
verses.where: Ruth, a widow from Moab who has come home with Naomi to Bethlehem, asks Naomi to let her go and glean in the fields, and she comes to the field of Boaz. The site's note on the chapter says Boaz protects her, feeds her, and quietly tells his workers to leave extra grain for her. The note on Deuteronomy 24 lists the law that left the forgotten sheaf for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow; a law kept generously fed two women with no wage.

verses.text: Give us this day our daily bread.
verses.where: In the prayer Jesus taught, the most ordinary need of the body, bread for today, is brought before the Father. The site's teaching note on the chapter says people who are poor or out of work should not hear its call not to worry as a suggestion that their need is their fault, and that the community of disciples is how the Father often answers this petition. The prayer is said in the plural.

verses.text: There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to visit them, and he stayed and worked with them because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was.
verses.where: In Corinth Paul stays and works with Aquila and Priscilla, tentmakers recently driven out of Rome by the emperor's order. The site's plain note says Paul paid his own way with a trade, and that this couple, driven out of their home, opened it to someone else. Work lost and work taken up again sit in the same verse as an open door.

verses.text: But I said, “I have labored in vain, I have spent My strength in futility and vanity; yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God.”
verses.where: The Servant of the LORD says he has labored in vain and spent his strength for nothing, yet his vindication is with the LORD. The site's note says he confesses that his labor seems wasted and still trusts God for his vindication, and God answers by giving him a larger task. Work that looks wasted to everyone else is not wasted to God.

verses.text: I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound. I am accustomed to any and every situation—to being filled and being hungry, to having plenty and having need. I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.
verses.where: Writing from prison, Paul says he has learned to be content with plenty and with need, and can do all things through Christ who gives him strength. The site's plain note says the strength is to be content, to go hungry without despair and to have plenty without pride, and that a person who has lost a job, their health or their plans can still say it truly. It promises Christ's strength in every circumstance, not a change of circumstance.

links.label: Practical guides for work and money

misread.taken: I have never seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread is taken as a promise that faithful people never lose their income, so that a believer out of work or going hungry must have done something wrong.
misread.says: The site's plain note says it is honest to say plainly that the righteous do sometimes go hungry, and that the Bible itself says so: a famine drove Naomi's family out of Bethlehem, and Lazarus was a beggar. Readers have taken the verse as one old man's witness to his own life, as a description of how a community keeping God's law usually helps the generous in trouble, or as a look ahead to the end of the story. The note rules out one use: it must never be used to say that poor people are poor because they are not righteous, and the psalm asks God's people to be the open hand that feeds.
misread.text: I once was young and now am old, yet never have I seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread.

whole: If losing your job has brought despair, thoughts of hurting yourself, or weeks of lost sleep and appetite, tell someone you trust today, a doctor, a pastor or a friend, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, with a page for people who have lost a job. Losing work takes more than a paycheck. People describe the meeting that lasted ten minutes, the box carried to the car, the first Monday at home with nowhere to be. Then come the bills, the dread of telling family, the forms, the applications that are never answered, and the question at every gathering about what you do now. Some feel shame they cannot explain; some are angry at a company that did not care; many feel both, and wonder whether God has stopped noticing.

Scripture does not treat this as small, and it does not treat it as proof of failure. The men in Jesus' parable were standing in the marketplace because no one had hired them, and the story never blames them. Joseph did everything right and was forgotten by the man he helped, for two more years. The Teacher of Ecclesiastes saw that bread does not always go to the wise, nor favor to the skillful, because time and chance happen to all. Part of the pain is that work had become more than work. A job gives a person a place to go, people who expect them, and a ready answer to the question of who they are, and when it is taken those things go with it. It is easy, then, to hear the loss as a verdict on your worth.

So the Bible's wisdom starts by refusing that verdict and then turns practical. Grieve it honestly, as a real loss. Pray for daily bread, in the plural, and let others help: the note on Matthew 6 says the community of disciples is how the Father often answers that prayer, and Ruth was fed through a law that let the poor glean and a landowner who kept it generously. Look for work steadily without letting the search swallow every hour, take up honest work where it can be found, as Paul made tents, and keep the rhythm of rest and worship that reminds you who you are when no one is paying you. Where bills and debts press, get sound advice early. And churches that read this should hear the psalm's own charge: be the open hand.

The hope Scripture gives is that God is not done with a person whose work has been taken. Joseph named his second son Ephraim, because God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction. The Servant said he had labored in vain, and still said his reward was with his God. Habakkuk could rejoice in God while the fields gave nothing. Paul learned to be content in want from a prison cell, and the strength he was given was not a change of circumstance but Christ in it. Your times are in God's hands, not in a company's, and the one who keeps going back to the marketplace has not stopped looking for you.
deep.sit: What has this loss made you believe about your worth, and what does God say instead?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says verse 15 is for days when life feels out of control: say it slowly, my times are in Your hands, not in your boss's, your doctor's or your enemy's.
prayer.text: But I trust in You, O LORD; I say, “You are my God.” My times are in Your hands; deliver me from my enemies and from those who pursue me. Make Your face shine on Your servant; save me by Your loving devotion.

careLines.text: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone.
Seeking help is not a failure of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
